unit.title: The Earth and the Moon
unit.blurb: The shapes and sizes of the Earth, the Sun and the Moon, the Moon's surface and its phases.

O1.t: Know that the Earth, the Sun and the Moon are spheres, and compare their sizes.

O2.t: Know that the Moon orbits the Earth, describe its surface, and know that moonlight is reflected sunlight.

O3.t: Name the phases of the Moon and know that the pattern repeats about every month.

captions: Hello, space explorers!
Let's blast off and look at the Earth, the Sun and the Moon!
This is lesson 6.1: the shapes of the Earth, the Sun and the Moon.
Three, two, one… blast off!
Our rocket zooms up into space.
Look back at the Earth.
It is round, like a ball! A ball shape is called a sphere.
The Earth is a sphere.
The Sun is a sphere too. It is a giant ball of very hot gas.
And the Moon is a sphere.
All three are shaped like balls!
Pause and think.
What shape is the Earth?
Which is the biggest?
The Moon is the smallest of the three.
The Earth is bigger than the Moon.
And the Sun is huge! More than a million Earths could fit inside it!
But the Sun looks small in the sky. Why?
Hold a ball close to your eyes. It looks big.
Now ask a friend to carry it far away.
It looks tiny! The Sun looks small because it is very, very far away.
Did you know?
The Sun is a star!
It is the closest star to us. The other stars are much further away.
Joke time!
How do you throw a party in space?
You planet!
Your turn.
Which is the biggest: the Earth, the Sun or the Moon?
Let's make a space model.
Find three balls of different sizes.
Use the biggest ball for the Sun, a small one for the Earth, and a tiny one for the Moon.
Line them up from smallest to biggest!
Let's remember.
The Earth, the Sun and the Moon are all spheres, like balls.
The Sun is the biggest.
The Moon is the smallest.
And the Sun is a star. Out-of-this-world work!

captions: Hello, space explorers!
Let's visit the Moon!
This is lesson 6.2: the Moon.
The Moon travels round and round the Earth.
We say the Moon orbits the Earth.
One trip round the Earth takes about one month.
Round and round it goes!
Pause and think.
What does the Moon travel around?
What is the Moon like?
It is covered in grey rocks and dust.
It has big round holes called craters.
There is no air to breathe, and no water to drink. Nothing lives on the Moon.
Long ago, a rocket flew all the way to the Moon.
Astronauts walked on the Moon! They wore space suits to breathe.
They left footprints in the dust.
There is no wind on the Moon, so the footprints are still there!
The Moon shines at night. But it does not make its own light!
Sunlight shines on the Moon.
The light bounces off the Moon.
Then it comes to our eyes. That is moonlight!
Did you know?
On the Moon, gravity is weaker.
You would feel very light, and you could bounce like a kangaroo!
Joke time!
Why did the cow jump over the Moon?
Because the farmer had cold hands!
Your turn.
Does the Moon make its own light?
Let's make Moon craters!
Fill a tray with flour, and sprinkle a little cocoa on top.
Drop marbles or small balls into the flour from up high.
Carefully lift them out. Look at your craters!
Let's remember.
The Moon orbits the Earth. One trip takes about a month.
The Moon has rocks, dust and craters.
There is no air and no water on the Moon.
And moonlight is sunlight bouncing off the Moon. Moon-tastic work!

captions: Hello, space explorers!
Why does the Moon change shape? Let's find out!
This is lesson 6.3: phases of the Moon.
Look at the Moon at night.
One night it is big and round.
A week later, it looks like half a circle.
Later, it is just a thin slice! The Moon seems to change shape.
But the Moon is always a round ball.
The Sun always lights up half of it.
As the Moon goes round the Earth, we see different amounts of the bright half.
These different shapes are called the phases of the Moon.
Pause and think.
Does the Moon really change shape?
Let's name some phases.
A new moon: we cannot see it at all!
A crescent moon: a thin slice, like a banana.
A half moon. And a full moon: a big, bright circle!
The phases go round in a pattern.
From a new moon, the bright part grows bigger and bigger.
After about two weeks, it is a full moon.
Then it gets smaller again, back to a new moon. One whole pattern takes about a month.
Did you know?
The word month comes from the word Moon!
A month is about how long the Moon takes to go through all its phases.
Joke time!
When is the Moon not hungry?
When it is full!
Your turn.
What do we call the Moon when it is a big, bright circle?
Let's keep a Moon diary!
Each night, look out of the window with an adult, and find the Moon.
Draw its shape in your diary. Do this for two weeks.
How did the Moon's shape change?
Let's remember.
The Moon seems to change shape, but it is always round.
The shapes are called phases.
Full moon, half moon, crescent and new moon.
And the pattern takes about a month. You have finished the Stage 3 lessons. Stellar work!
